Exploratory Data Analysis for Machine Learning¶

Module 5: Final Project¶

Telco Customer Churn Data Analysis

Dataset source: https://community.ibm.com/community/user/blogs/steven-macko/2019/07/11/telco-customer-churn-1113

A fictional telco company which provided phone and internet services has a dataset of 7043 customers. It contains information of customers such as senior status, gender, and other features. The target of this dataset is the churn outcome of each customer, saying whether they churned or not.

In this project, we will import the data, handle any missing data, perform EDA, and hypothesis testing.

Hypothesis Testing¶

Hypothesis #1¶

Maybe the age of the customers is a factor in whether they churn or not.

$ 𝐻_{0} $: Senior proportions are not significantly different between churning and non-churning customers.

$ 𝐻_{A} $: Senior proportions are different between churning and non-churning groups.

In [17]:
contingency= pd.crosstab(churn_data.SeniorCitizen, churn_data.Churn)
contingency
Out[17]:
Churn No Yes
SeniorCitizen
No 4508 1393
Yes 666 476

The bar graph below depicts the distribution of churn by senior status. This will allow us to compare the distribution of customers among the churn groups and senior status.

In [18]:
contingency.plot(kind='bar')
plt.title("Churn Distribution by Senior Citizen Status")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.xlabel("Senior Citizen?")
Out[18]:
Text(0.5, 0, 'Senior Citizen?')

The majority of customers are not senior citizens. In both groups, the number of those who have not churned are greater than those who have. Among senior citizens however, the number of churned and not churned are closer. A chi-squared hypothesis test will allow us to see if senior status is a significant factor in determining churn outcome.

In [19]:
chi2, p_val, dof, exp_freq = chi2_contingency(contingency, correction = False)
print('chi-square statistic: {} , p_value: {} , degree of freedom: {} ,expected frequencies: {} '.format(chi2, p_val, dof, exp_freq))

chi-square statistic: 160.35213184520632 , p_value: 9.477903507376051e-37 , degree of freedom: 1 ,expected frequencies: [[4335.05239245 1565.94760755]
 [ 838.94760755  303.05239245]]
In [20]:
if (p_val < 0.05):
    print('Reject the null hypothesis, that senior proportions are not significantly different between churning and non-churning customers.')
else:
    print('Accept the null hypothesis, that senior proportions are not significantly different between churning and non-churning customers.')

Reject the null hypothesis, that senior proportions are not significantly different between churning and non-churning customers.

Since we rejected the null hypothesis, we can conclude that there is an association between senior status and churn outcome.

Hypothesis #2¶

Perhaps the price of the services was the reason why our customers churned. It could be reasoned that the customers who churned were charged more than those who didn't. To thest this theory, the hypothesis testing below is carried out.

$ 𝐻_{0}:\mu_{1}<=\mu_{2} $ The average monthly charges of customers who churned are less than or equal to customers who didn't churn.

$ 𝐻_{A}:\mu_{1}>\mu_{2} $ The average monthly charges of customers who churned are greater than customers who didn't churn.

Conclusion: since p_value 1.3533228034442077e-60 is less than alpha 0.05 
Reject the null hypothesis that the average monthly charges of customers who churned are less than or equal to customers who didn't churn.

Since we reject the null hypthesis, we can conclude that the average monthly charges of customers who churned are greater than those who didn't churn. Therefore, pricing can be a factor that leads to customer churn. This may lead to a reconsideration of pricing or further investigation into why the churning individuals were being charged at higher prices.

Hypothesis #3¶

Could the contract type have an effect on churn outcome? This will be worth investigating to see whether the company should change its contract policies or not.

$ 𝐻_{0} $: The proportion of churning customers are not significantly different across the different contract types.

$ 𝐻_{A} $: Churning customer proportions are significantly different across contract types.

Conclusion¶

The Data¶

The Telco Customer Churn is a subset from a larger IBM dataset and was analyzed for EDA and hypothesis testing. The dataset contains customer information and their churn outcome.

What We Found¶

No missing values were found, being indicative that the data may have been already cleaned or was collected well. The majority of customers in the dataset have not churned. The highest rate of churn appears in customers who have been with the company for only 1 month.

Through chi-squared hypothesis testing, we found that the senior status of customers affects the churn outcome, as there is a siginificant difference in proportion in churn outcome by senior status. Additionally, a t-test showed that the average monthly charges of customers who churned were greater than those who did not. This means that cost is a significant factor in churn outcome. Lastly, the proportion of churning and not churning customers are significantly different across contract types, as was discovered via chi-squared testing.

Next Steps¶

More hypothesis tests can be done with the rest of the categorical variables available, to see if they are also significant factors in churn outcome. Multivariate tests may also be done. A more comprehensive dataset that contains more features may help with factors such as exact age and geographical location.

With logistic regression, we can find out what threshold of monthly cost can make the difference between a customer who will churn and one who won't. It would also be worth finding out how long it will take for a customer to be with the company to make them less likely to churn.
